I am 65 years old. I started farming when I was twenty, so I have forty-five years doing this. I only went to primary school, but I know my land. My family has four people and 7.7 mu. I grow wheat and maize on 5 mu — same plot, wheat in winter then maize in summer after we harvest the wheat in June. The other 2.7 mu is cotton. Quzhou ground is good for cotton, I have grown it a long time.

I do what worked last year. I watch my neighbors. Old Li across the way uses about the same fertilizer as me, and his crops always look strong, so I copy him. For wheat, I use improved seed. I rotary till the ground first. For fertilizer, I put one 50-kilogram bag of compound fertilizer on each mu before planting. Then in spring when the wheat turns green, I spread half a bag of urea on each mu. That is about 20 kilograms of nitrogen per mu total. I know it might be a little more than needed, but I would rather waste some fertilizer than lose yield. A bad harvest is a disaster. I irrigate three times: before winter freeze, at jointing, and when the grain is filling. I spray pesticide twice. I expect about 450 kilograms per mu if the weather is decent.

For maize, I plant hybrid seed straight into the wheat stubble after harvest, no deep tillage. I put about 60 jin of compound fertilizer in the rows when planting, then topdress with 50 jin of urea per mu when the plants are knee-high. That works out to about 16 kilograms of nitrogen per mu. I irrigate twice, maybe three times if it is very dry. Two pesticide sprays. I expect around 550 kilograms per mu.

For cotton, I rotary till first. I plant improved seed. I use one bag of compound fertilizer per mu as base, then add more urea twice during the growing season. Cotton needs more potassium, so I make sure the fertilizer has enough — I end up using about 8 kilograms of potassium per mu. I irrigate three times and spray four times because bollworm always comes. I expect about 280 kilograms of seed cotton per mu.

Everything costs money. Fertilizer, seed, pesticide, electricity for the well — it all adds up. But I have learned that trying to save too much on inputs is foolish. I adjust a little from last year, but not much. Change is risky.
